Flying from Hongkong to Hankow
Oct. 25, 1937.
Dear Family:
Am now on a trip which promises to be a very interesting one and
so for my own amusement and to continue my long neglected family letters
"I'll write as I please."
Mr. Bond and I left
Hongkong at 11:55 this morning.
We are flying
in a tri-motored Junkers operated by the Sino-German Eurasia Company.
men and two women, also a full load of air express including 175 lbs. of
anti-toxin consigned to the American Ambassador at Nanking.
The latter
shipment came over from the U.S. by Pan American and is carried free of
It is somewhat gratifying to one in
the business - temporarily resident in China - to see aircraft put to
good constructive use after viewing and reading about all the destructive
and cruel uses to which airplanes have lately been put in china.
Our take-off was bumpy as are most take-offs from the pocket-like
Hongkong airport surrounded by high mountains.
Climbed through low
ground haze and broken white fluffy clouds at 3000 feet and now, having
crossed infamous Bias Bay (where the Chinese pirates have given way to
the more legal but equally piratical Japs), we are flying over Chinese
territory. Down below are rugged brown mountains completely deforested
sides seared and torn by the rush of mad streams born of the torrential
rains which come in the
typhoon season.
In the valleys small Chinese
villages furnish shelter for the coolle farmers who cultivate every inch
of soil washed down from the mountains.
The little valleys look very
peaceful and viewing them I can understand why many of our Chinese
friends have sent their families "back to the country". Those little
villages are not worth a Japanese serial bomb - no army occupation of
this country is even threatened and those little villages are probably
safer than ever before because the war lords are all busy and will not
march their hordes of Chinese soldiers through this section.
We are well away from the coast now flying at 7000 feet - clouds
have all disappeared and an Arizona sky stretches from one haze covered
horizon to the other.
We have not sighted any other airplanes and I'll
be pertectly happy it none are encountered - of either side! Our pilot
reports, nowever,
that the Hankow Field - our objective - was bombed
light before last by Japanese planes - hangar destroyed - three Chinese
bombers on the ground and our poor old Western Division of PAA Ford
"loaned" to the Chinese Army were all burned up.
Unfortunately, the
bombers were a German made Heinkle, an Italian made Savoia-Machett1 (sp !)
and an American made Martin, all badly needed by the Chinese,
and among
the last of the good planes
they had left.
The pilot also says the
field is full of shell holes but all holes are clearly marked with red
flags and several runways are marked out for safe landing areas so there
is nothing to worry about. Bond reminds me that it 1s now 1:30 and that
our Chinese No.1 at Hongkong sent some lunch boxes to us, so we'll have
chow and I'll continue this letter later on.
Later - in fact after a good lunch of fried chicken, sandwiches,
hot coffee and cake, I lit a cigarette, tilted my chair back, enjoyed
a smoke and took a short siesta.
My box also contained some cold salad
but I passed that up.
There is
still some cholera in Hongkong). It 1s
now 2:30 PM and we are now about 375 miles northwest of Hongkong

#3
Oct. 28th.
This morning Harry Smith, the pilot who supplied
the pheasants, had another treat for us.
Smith used to fly for
chiang-Kai-shek.
Yesterday he bumped into an. acquaintance attached
to the Generalissimo's entourage.
The party in question had Just
returned from Hami, & city in far western Sinkiang Province where
he had secured for
the Generalissimo - either as an incident to,
or the objective of, his excursion, some Hami melons.
he gave unbeknownst to c.K.s.) to
Harry Smith.
In the old days the
chinese emperors used to operate a pony express from Hami to Peking
during the melon season.
The horsemen, descendants of Genghis Khan's
cavalrymen, rode night and day to rush
the melons to the Capital.
can well understand.
The melon 1s like a honey dew, only much better.
They are the size of small watermelon.
The mean is firm and crisp.
They are perfectly delicious, but apparently cannot be raised anywhere
else in the world except around Hami.
We had a busy time today. A morning long session with our CNAC
partners going over the business of the last two months since the
the afternoon we journeyed across the Yangssze to Wuchang to visit
the airplane factory which was moved here after the Japs attacked it
at Hangchow.
It was very interesting as
we were shown around by one
of our old men, Wong Su;
and he told us all about the bombing of
Hangehow - a hectic move by truck, train, river and coolle power.
Tonight we dine at 8 with the American Consul, Mr.Josselyn.
am going to mail this letter now by Eurasia to Hongkong and from there
by Clipper to my secretary Miss Forbes, who is staying with the family
at Baguio. She will make a number of
typewritten copies and mail from
the Phillippines.
Another installment will follow some time soon.
We are leaving tomorrow, Oct.28th, for Nanking, by British steamer.
There it will not be so quiet and peaceful as here but I think quite
safe. Conditions on the spot are never as bad as the newspapers would
lead you to believe. The further removed from the scene the worse
the reports.
As ever,
н. м.В.

We haven't heard anything further from Harold, but trust the next
He did remember
Manila Bay.
was very good and our first since han leaving China.
yours are keeping well.

Section 2
Wednesday PM, October 27,1937.
Dear Family:
It's 9 PM. Mr.Bond and I have just boarded the good ship
Kung Wo at Hankow.
We each have a large spacious cabin and we are
both turning in before the ship sails.
trying all day to make our Chinese associates understand a business
proposal which would be quite easy for a twelve year old child to
mater in half an hour? Such work 1s what irks one in China.
to whom we were talking represent the type with whom we must do business.
are completely worn out.
Thursday.
October 2sth.
Have just been ashore at KinKlang to look see
China shops.
Bought two small porcelain pictures just to have purchased
something where the best modern porcelain is made.
All day we have
travelled along the broad Yangtze, stopping only at Anking about six
o'clock PM.
There we anchored and a huge sampan, alive with Chinese,
came alongside,
tied up to our boat while amidst a scene of utmost chaos
a huge amount of practically worthless cargo came on board, including
about 100 coolies.
An approximately similar number got off with an
inferno of walla walla and confusion of small baskets, bundles and boxes.
Four young wounded soldiers were interesting.
They were Nanking boys
wounded in the fighting in the north and were being sent back to their
families in Nanking.
None of them looked to be over sixteen years old.
There are only four first class passengers on this large river boat -
the other two are Chinese, one bound for Wuhu where we land early tomorrow
morning, and the other for Chinkiang, a town just upstream from the boom
which the Chinese have stretched across the Yangtze to keep the Jap fleet
out of the river.
Our Captain and his first mate - both Britishers -
say the boom is an effective bar to navigation.
It is composed of old
hulks filled with stones and sunk side by side clear across the river.
Below the boom an extensive system of mines makes it dangerous to even
approach the boom.
The small Chinese boats can get around the boom
through a series of canals and are busy carrying Shanghai cargo around
the boom,
which cargo is delivered then to English boats which carry it
in either direction to or away from Shanghai.
riday, October 29th.
Went to bed at 9 PM and didn't wake up until 8 AM
see I'm not suffering from insomnia.
This morning there is a cold
wind blowing from the north.
have just
left Wuhu and are due at
Nanking about noon.
The weather is bad - which is good - because the
Japs can't bomb with a low ceiling.
If they fly low the anti-airerait
guns shoot them down and if they fly high they can't see Nanking because
there is a solid overcoat at about 3000 feet.
Also since International
pressure has been exerted against indiscriminate bombing, that type of
attack has been practiced only against cities and towns where there are
no influential foreigners.
-4-
68801 SINOS

#5
Saturday, October 30th.
We arrived at Nanking without incident. The
boat docked about three miles upstream
from the Nanking Bund and we
transferred to a tug which brought us (standing in the fain on front
dock) to the dock.
There we hired the most disreputable looking old
Ford taxi and set
out for the American Embassy.
The main drag (Chang
Shan Road) is lined with bomb shelters.
Otherwise the capital seems
as quiet and untouched by war as before the present hostilitles began.
Several bomb scars have akast since been pointed out to me but craters
have been filled and no signs of damage are discernible. None of the
large public buildings has been hit though many have been the target of
air raids.
We are living at the American Embassy with Mr. Peck who very
kindly invited us to live with him during our stay in Nanking. Last
night Mr.Peck had a dinner party with Ambassador Johnson, a Dr. and Mrs.
Hershberg and their twenty year old daughter.
They were
very charming
Germans who all spoke excellent English.
Dr. Hershberg 1s a famous
surgeon who has done some remarkable operations and is helping tremen-
dously in the present Chinese hospital management. It is suspected
that he left a good practice in Germany to avoid persecution by Hitlerites.
After äinner we played "Poker Patience". There was no bomb raiå as the
bad weather continued.
Sunday AM, October 31st.
Yesterday was also a bad day - therefore a
Our managing Director arrived from Hankow having been unable
to join us Friday because the airplane schedule was cancelled that day
account weather.
We had
a session with him - went to dinner at the
International Club where most of the foreigners remaining in Nanking
congregate every Saturday night to make a little whoople up to curfew
time at 11 PM.
I met many old friends there and had a fine time.
There was only one woman present - a French girl who arrived here a few
weeks ago as a volunteer nurse - fell in love with a French newspaper
correspondent and was married night before last. The whole town turned
out for the weading.
Women in Nanking are so scarce that whenever you
see one you stamp your hand as the kids do when they see a white horse.
About 80% of the foreign population of Nanking has gone.
I had a long talk with Mr. Holm, a good friend of ours,
who used
to be Postal Commissioner at Chungking.
He has resigned and is keen on
returning with Mrg.Holm to his "home" in Copenhagen after thirty years
in China. I wonder if they won't soon want to come back. Here, for
at Chungking, Mr. Holm was a real personage.
He lived
beautiful Chinese house (provided rent free by the Post Office) sur.
rounded by a lovely garden.
He travelled to work in a grand sedan chair
fitted out like a small throne, borne by four uniformed chair coolies.
He had a No.1 boy who ran the house and looked after every detail from
food to pressing his suits and shining his boots.
Several coolies were
at his beck and call to run errands, bring him whatever he called for, etc.
Three gardeners cared for his garden as though it were their own. It
will be different in Copenhagen.
Later - Sunday night - rain and low ceiling all day. Had long
conference with Vice-Minister of Communications which lasted all morning
and accomplished nothing.
Very discouraging.
Lunch with Mr.Peck and
Mr. Johnson, also dinner - much conversation but no results.
American
attitude very sympathetic and helpful, Chinese very unsympatnetic and
non-co-operative.
Some Chinese officials can be unbelievably dull and
stupid.
Our friend of today's conference seems intent only on immediate
necessities to the exclusion of all else. Hope for better luck tomorrow.
988ONSI

#6
We have been here now two and one half days with no air attack
which probably means a strong one or more tomorrow, unless of course,
this weather continues.
There is an air of expectancy in Nanking, a
sort of indefinite tenseness which must get on everyone's nerves
sooner or later.
Possibly they get used to it and probably I would
too, but frankly, I'll be glad to get away.
W1ll send this letter by Tuesday's plane to Hankow with the
hope that it will catch Eurasia to Hongkong Wednesday and the Clipper
to Manila on Thursday. Next installment will follow later.
We get little news here except about the Shanghai front and
even that is mixed with all sorts of wild rumors.
Weren't the Japs
showing their real nature when they fired at the
"doomed battalion"
when they evacuated that warehouse and surrendered to the British
for internment? Those dirty little Japs haven't any decent traits.
Why didn't they cease firing and give those Chinese a rousing cheer
when they evacuated? That would have been sporting - but not at all
Japanese.
Tuesday, November 2,1931
If I remember correctly, this letter was started with the state-
ment that we were
embarking on a trip which might prove exciting.
Probably I too was a victim of newspaper stories which depict a war
torn China, the air filled with Japanese planes raining bombs on
detenceless Chinese cities. As a matter of fact, we flew across 600
miles of China skies from Hongkong to Hankow without seeing a Japanese
plane - and now after more than a week in war torn China we have yet
Manking that hundreds of bombe have been
Even here at
is difficult to
find any trace of damage.
This morning we had an air raid alarm, but
soon the "all clear" signal was given, and no planes or bombs were
heard.
Wednesday,
November 3rd.
No excitement today except one air rala
Walked over to the Embassy office across the road from Mr. Peck's
and inspected the U.S. dug out - very muddy, dark and full of
mosquitos.
Think when the raids come I'll take my chances outside.
A direct hit will get you either in or out of that hole in the ground.
If you are outside and lie flat, you are just about as well off and
lots more comfortable.
Bond left tonight by motor car for Shanghai.
Many cars are constantly going back and forth, mostly at night, in
order to avoid Jap airplanes machine-gunning them on the road.
friend of ours left his car as a plane approached and ran out
field where there was a Chinese grave mound.
The plane dove at him,
but he stayed in the lee of the mound until it passed - then he noticed
the Jap turn and come back at him, so he ran around the other side of
the mound - again in the lee. This performance was repeated during six
attacks, after which the Jap flew off, probably out of ammunition.
I hope Bond doesn't have any such experience. He is coming back on

Sunday.
In the meantime I am working on a lot of reports and proposals
requested by the Chinese officials with whom we are trying to deal. If
patience 1s a virtue, we are among the most virtuous alive.
I'hursday,
November 4th.
Rained hard all day. Low ceiling, no possi-
bility of air raid. News from Shanghai very bad. Have been pounding
terror ll day bern m Balls don to his secretary,
"Miss Ella go slow
because I'm in a helluva hurry". There 1s absolutely
no chance of getting a
rellable typist in Nanking - all the Embassy people
are writing their own
letters and those who know how to operate a type-
writer are fortunate.
Bond radioed over CMAC system this morning that he arrived at
Shanghai safely without incident.
Mr. Peck 1s having a farewell dinner for Mr. Holm tonight.
Friday, November 5th.
Nice party last night with two ladies present -
occurrence in Nanking these days.
Mr. and Mrs. Richie, No.1 for-
eigner in the Post Office, Mr. Holm, Mr.and Mrs.MeDaniel, a newspaper man
and Ambassador Johnson.
Today has been another rainy day with low
ceiling.
Have been here a week with not a single air raid. Ordinarily
a week of rainy weather 1s hard to take, but here a bright sunny day is
ushered in with curses. Have to see one of the Secretaries of the Ministry
of Finance tomorrow.
Their Administration building was bombed and while
not badly damaged, they are all afraid to go back and are now quartered
in the Ministry of Railways building temporarily while a bomb proof air
conditioned concrete underground office is being constructed next door
to the American Embassy.
Saturday, November 6th. Another low overcast rainy day.
When we were
to operate a regular airline, such stretches of weather were the
bane of our existence.
This weather is all the more remarkable for
the fall is usually the only good weather season in this section of China.
Today I was grateful for that low ceiling as I had to spend the morning
in the Ministry of Railways Building, itself normally the target for
bomb attacks located as it is on the main street with the $12,000,000
Ministry of Communications Building just across the street but even more
of a target now because shared by two other Ministries, Finance and
Industry.
However, even with good weather I suspect Nanking 1s reasonably
safe from indiscriminate bombing until after the Nine Power Treaty con-
versations are concluded.
We do hear persistent rumors that the Capital
will be "leveled to the ground". These rumors have been especially current
during the last few days.
Sunday, November 7th. Another gray day with solid overcast at 2000 feet -
a disappointing talk with high Chinese official. The Chinese, as has been
rightly said,
are traders - not merchants. They are where they are because
they will not look far enough ahead.
Sincerely,

#8
Nanking, November 8, 1937.
Dear Family:
Today was bright and clear - not a cloud in the sky.
Japs bombed a passenger train north of here killing two hundred innocent
non-combattants,
but they didn't bomb Nanking, for which no doubt we have
the Brussels conference
to thank.
Mr. Peck
and I had dinner with some
old friends, Mr. and Mrs.Pan of the Ministry of Railways.
esting to hear
first hand of the marvelous job the railroads are doing -
they keep the trains moving under almost impossible odds.
In one instance
over 1000 bombs of various sizes were dropped on one short stretch of
track but within twelve hours trains were again operating over that stretch
of roadbed.
The repair crews work at night and sleep in dugouts during
the day time.
At Soochow they had an average of eight hours of bombing
for ten conescutive days, but
still kept the trains moving.
If that sort
of morale can pervade all services,
the Japs are going to have a long and
tough job ahead.
November 9th.
Beautiful day - no bomb raids. Chinese are asking bide
on 60 basic trainer airplanes - they must think the war will last a long
time. The Board meeting was postponed until tomorrow - d--- it! I had
planned to leave tomorrow.
Bond can't get back to Nanking by car because
all roads are blocked.
He wired that he was coming by British boat and
driving by car around the boom in the Langtsze.
He expects to arrive
here on Friday or Saturday.
Will probably wait until he comes as the
boat I was planning to take icaves tomorrow morning and there probably
will not be another until the one he comes on.
Someone - probably a paint salesman - sold the Chinese on the
idea of painting all their bullaings a dirty gray color - supposedly so
they will not be so conspicuous from the air.
Of course, all the bombing
is done from great heights and about the only thing the bomber can see is
roofs - but nearly every building is covered with that awful looking stuff -
even statues, Ming Tomb Memorial and the Ningxim Sun Yat Sen Memorial.
Don't know why the Japs overlooked that Memorial and the Ming Tombs, but
though outside the wall, neither of these "military objectives" have been
bombed.
I predict they will be, and when a howl is raised, the Japs will
say that anti-aircraft guns were there.
Of course, the Chinese have been
very careful not to give the Japanese any valla reason for bombing the tomb
of their George Washington.
Dined tonight with some of the American teachers at Nanking
University and some missionaries.
It was easy to tell which were which -
most of the teachers took a cocktail and smoked.
The missionaries may
do both - like a debutante raiüing the ice-box when she gets home - but
with the Ambassador and Mr. Peck both present, they were on their best
behavior and wore the proper funereal gravity which 1s the mode among
missionaries when there is laughter or anyone is having a good time.
Wednesday, November 10th.
As I write this I am waiting for a meeting
of the Board of Directors of CNAC - the meeting was called for 3 o'clock
but on arriving punctually I am told in true,
very polite Chinese fashion
that the meeting will not be held until 4. Of course, they did not think
to call me up. At noon we had an air raid - the first alarm came at 12:20 -

a long siren followed by the beating on brass gongs around town at
strategic points, so even the soundly sleeping chauffers of waiting
motor cars are awakened.
The celling was about six thousand feet
and above that a solid overcast.
Three Jap planes came in from the
east, flew directly over the city in a V formation.
They flew
directly over the American Embassy and released their bombs soon
after crossing over.
Their target was the military air fields from
which all airplanes have long since departed.
The hangars are already
a shambles and coolies repair the field
as fast as the Japs can hit it.
Ine oninese at Hangkow, and possibly here, build wood and paper air-
planes which they park at random around the edges of the field. The
Japs drop tons of bombs, costing thousands of dollars,
and report the
destruction of say ten enemy planes.
That night the Chinese kite makers
rebuild their paper planes, move them to new positions and the next day
the process is repeated. In this manner the Japanese have reported the
destruction of more airplanes than the Chinese ever owned. I suppose
the Japanese Foreign office will soon start issuing claims of "non-co-
operation" and"insincerity" and threaten to "take measures".
As the planes went over the city the anti-aircrait guns cut
loose from every side and machine guns rattled like the sound of driving
rivets.
The anti-aircraft shells maûe black puffs of smoke in the gray
sky arouna the planes, but none exploded near enough to do any damage
and the planes nela their formation and their course seemingly undis-
turbed by the noise chorus from below. The bombs were dropped inside
ine wall which encircles the city.
here in this room all lights are out and there is no heat.
am writing next to a window, one of two such openings with a door between,
a small amount of light filters in Irom
the courtyard over the double row
o: sand bage piled celling high in front of the door and windows.
room is one set aside for meetings and conferences.
It is on the firgt
floor of the four storied magnificent Ministry of Communications building
built in modern steel and concrete to resemble the old Chinese architec-
ture. I am told that the floor above us is bomb-proof. I hope that
statement is true for the siren outside is at this moment screaming the
signal which warns that another raid is on the way.
Outposts with
telephone connections to the siren stations are flung around Nanking in
a circle so that warnings are given about 15 minutes before the planes get
here.
To augment the siren a small boy walked through the corridor with
an alarm clock ringing vociferously the while he wound it vigorously.
Literally an alarm clock!
We had our board meeting in the candle light -
all lights are off during raids - and I'll confess that it was a bit eerie
and disconcerting until we got the "all clear" signal, when lights were
turned on and it was again a case of business as usual. The Ministry
Building is checked as an objective on all the Jap maps which have been
taken from planes shot down.
Our meeting was a total loss so far as
getting anything accomplished along lines desired by us.
Had dinner at the Metropolitan Hotel with some of my American
aviation iriends
all of whom are here trying to get "their share" (meaning
In each case all) of an order for seven million U.S.dollars worth of air-
planes, motors and parts.
They are all worried about deliveries and their
schemes are legion for beating the Japanese blockade and various American
restrictive export regulations. The Board Room is a large square room with
-9-

#10
four alcoves off the center - in one of which I am writing near the
sandbag-barricaded window.
The candles threw a flickering light
partially illuminating the room and revealing the midnight blue
posts which support a ceiling decorated with gold medalioned filled
small squares against a rich dark red background with cross beams
covered with designs of red, green, blue and yellow. The center of
the square room was taken up by a table around which we were seated.
Bond did not get back, so I was the only "barbarian" present.
ThursdaY.
Armistice Day - only in history.
This noon
cut loose at the same time as
yesterday and 15 minutes
the drone of many motors was audible but no planes in sight. Mr. Johnson
Mr. Peck and I left the tiffin table and repaired to a little open porch
near the roof. Next to Mr. Peck's house, in which I am staying, 1s a
large Chinese grave yard with lots of mounds which provide good shelter
against flying shrapnel. The nearby Chinese Tarmers, ricksha coolles
and servants all congregate there when an alarm sounds. They come there
for the cover afforded by the hundreds of grave mounds and also to be
near the American flag which they at least think affords them some
measure of protection.
The noise of the motors became louder and
presently out of the clouds to the south three Japanese twin-motored
came into view - below the clouds at about 6000 feet. The sky
was about 95 percent overcast at that altitude and only infrequent
holes showed
a light blue against the gray which of course predominated.
The Three bombers came directly at us,
then turned away toward the
airport outside the wall, where no doubt more paper planes had been
constructed by those overworked kite-makers. Machine guns tack-tack-
anti-aircraft guns banged from all quarters and the boom of
exploding shells overhead kept us under a protruding edge of the roof
as pieces of shrapnel fell around us.
It's wise to keep under some
protective covering, for the fragmentation is not always complete and
a spent bit oi shell can give you quite a jolt it it is a large piece
that drops on you.
The Three bombers in V
formation dropped their
bombs on the airport and in the din of rapid explosions we could see
clouds of dust rising against the horizon some half mile away.
pursuit planes followed and just messed around, one of them stunting
while the other two stayed more or less in formation. One of the
bombers left formation and heading directly over the city. Mr. Peck
opined that he was probably going to bomb the City inside the wall,
but instead he again flew directly over us, turned and once more
headed for the airport, possibly to check the number of "planes"
destroyed.
As he flew over the city wall an anti-aircraft shell burst
close to him and we noted a bit of smoke come from the ship just as it
disappeared into some clouds. Suddenly we were amazed to hear a lot of
shouts and hand-clapping
(a new form of expressing approval among Chinese)
from the grave-yard and looking where they were all excitedly gazing,
we saw a streak of black smoke - then a blazing mass which broke into
two brightly burning meteors which continued downward through live thousand
feet to hit, still in flames, near the airport.
The Japs had traded some
Nippon copy of a Douglas all-metal airplane with crew of six for a few
paper ones! Great rejoicing in Nanking but I guess it's a different
story in six Tokyo homes! However, they died for "Charley" and we'll let
him worry about that!
Friday November 12tn.
Another rainy day. Trees sticking up into
celling. Plan to leave tomorrow by boat from Hankow.
